Pip’s little reef book

A home made by tiny animals.

A coral colony is many tiny animals called polyps. Reef-building corals make hard skeletons that offer shelter to other life.

Meet real coral ↗

Your hands join the chorus.

Moving waste or coral: pinch to carry, then open your hand to place it. Or hold your hand still over an object to pick it up, carry it, then hold over its destination.

With hands armed, point one finger near a stem, then trace your branch. Open your hand to finish. Or wave gently to grow a branch. Hold your hand over a button for one second to choose it. Fish approach and awaken its notes. Each coral crown adds another part to your ocean music.

Real reef crackles come largely from snapping shrimp and fishes. Our piano and bronze notes are an artistic interpretation.Listen to the science ↗

New growth takes living tissue—and care.

Heat can bleach coral. A blast breaks habitat. A surviving living fragment can grow a new colony. Dead skeletons cannot be revived.

We compress months or years into a short story. Real restoration needs trained teams, suitable sites, monitoring and fewer pressures.How restoration works ↗

Care is a practice, not one click.

In this story, sweep algae from the nursery supports, hold both ties, then inspect the three growing tips. You are helping a living fragment grow a new colony.

Real teams clean nursery structures, secure fragments without damaging living tissue, and check health and water conditions over months or years. Never take or handle wild coral yourself.Meet real coral gardeners ↗

A reef has a soundscape.

Real reefs contain fish calls and snapping-shrimp crackles. Healthy reef sounds can help some young corals settle.

Here, visiting animals awaken piano or bronze notes in your coral. Those musical notes are an artistic translation, not sounds made by coral skeletons.

The soundscape research ↗

Every neighbour needs a place.

Pip is a small chromis, a fish associated with branching reefs. Cardinalfish hover in sheltered places; crabs find cover in crevices.

Anemonefish need a suitable host anemone—an anemone is an animal, but it is not a coral. Seagrasses are flowering plants rooted in sand or mud, not soft corals.

The paper reef is inspired by the Indo-Pacific, including Indonesia. Not every visitor appears immediately: shelter grows first.Explore reef habitats ↗
